title: Networking 15: Socket Programming with UDP and TCP

questions.q: In the Internet architecture, what is a socket?
choices: A physical connector on the network interface card
The door between an application process and the end-to-end transport protocol
A table a router uses to forward packets
A link-layer buffer that holds frames before transmission
questions.explain: A socket is the interface (door) between the application layer program and the transport layer underneath it. It is the only API between application code and the Internet's transport services.

questions.q: In a host's protocol stack, which part is controlled by the application developer rather than by the operating system?
choices: The transport layer
The network and link layers
The application process
Everything above the physical layer
questions.explain: Application programs run in user space, outside the OS. The transport layer and everything below it are inside the operating system. The socket sits between the two.

questions.q: Which of these describe the service a TCP socket gives an application?
choices: Reliable data transfer
Bytes delivered in order, as a stream
Flow control and congestion control
No handshake before data is sent
The destination address must be attached to every message
questions.explain: TCP provides reliable, in-order byte-stream transfer with flow and congestion control. Skipping the handshake and attaching a destination address to every packet are properties of UDP.

questions.q: From the application's point of view, what does UDP provide?
choices: Reliable, in-order byte-stream transfer
Reliable datagrams that may arrive out of order
Unreliable transfer of groups of bytes (datagrams) between client and server processes
A connection set up by a handshake, but with no reliability
questions.explain: UDP is an unreliable datagram service with no connection. Datagrams may be lost or arrive out of order.

questions.q: The Internet provides a directory service where a client can look up which server offers a service and which port it listens on.
questions.explain: The Internet has no such directory. The client simply has to know the server's host name (or IP address) and port number. A host name is then translated to an IP address with DNS.

questions.q: What is the well-known port number of a DNS server?
questions.explain: Well-known ports include 80 for HTTP, 25 for SMTP and 53 for DNS.

questions.q: Which pairing of protocols with their well-known port numbers is correct?
choices: HTTP: 25, SMTP: 80
HTTP: 80, SMTP: 25
HTTP: 53, SMTP: 25
HTTP: 80, SMTP: 53
questions.explain: HTTP uses port 80, SMTP uses port 25 and DNS uses port 53.

questions.q: A client knows only a server's host name, not its IP address. What has to happen before packets can be addressed to the server?
choices: The client broadcasts the host name and waits for the server to answer
The host name is translated to an IP address by a query to the local DNS server
The server registers itself with the client's operating system
Nothing: the network layer routes packets by host name
questions.explain: Packets are addressed by IP address, so a host name has to be resolved through DNS first.

questions.q: With UDP sockets, the client and server perform a handshake before any application data is sent.
questions.explain: UDP has no connection between client and server, so there is no handshake before data is sent.

questions.q: Why does a UDP sender have to attach the destination IP address and port number to every packet it sends?
choices: UDP encrypts each packet separately
UDP requires the server to acknowledge each packet
There is no connection between client and server, so the socket has no fixed destination
The operating system changes the destination port after every packet
questions.explain: Without a connection, the UDP socket isn't tied to a particular peer, so every datagram has to carry its destination address and port explicitly (for example, the address argument to sendto()).

questions.q: When a UDP server receives a datagram, how does it learn where to send its reply?
choices: It looks up the client in a DNS directory
It extracts the sender's IP address and port number from the received packet
It reads them from the connection set up during the handshake
It always replies to port 12000 on the client
questions.explain: The receiver extracts the sender's IP address and port from the received packet. In Python, recvfrom() returns them as clientAddress, and the server passes that to sendto().

questions.q: Data sent over a UDP socket may be lost or may arrive out of order.
questions.explain: UDP is unreliable: transmitted data may be lost or received out of order.

questions.q: In socket(AF_INET, SOCK_DGRAM), what does SOCK_DGRAM specify?
choices: The socket uses IPv4
The socket is a TCP socket
The socket is a UDP (datagram) socket
The socket will be bound to a well-known port
questions.explain: SOCK_DGRAM gives you a UDP datagram socket. SOCK_STREAM gives you a TCP socket. AF_INET is the argument that means an IPv4 Internet socket.

questions.q: In a socket() call, what does AF_INET indicate?
choices: An Internet socket that uses IPv4
A UDP socket
A socket that works only on the local machine
A socket bound to port 80
questions.explain: When sockets were invented there were many kinds of network layers. AF_INET picks an Internet socket that uses IP version 4.

questions.q: A UDP client has to call bind() to choose a port number before it can send a datagram.
questions.explain: The client doesn't give a port number when it creates its socket. The operating system assigns one. A client can call bind() if it wants a specific port, but it doesn't have to.

questions.q: In the example UDP server, which socket does the server use to send its reply?
choices: A new socket created for each client
A socket created by recvfrom()
The same serverSocket it reads datagrams from
The client's socket, which arrives inside the datagram
questions.explain: A UDP server reads from and writes to the same socket (serverSocket). It names the client's address in each sendto() call.

questions.q: Why does the UDP server call bind() while the UDP client doesn't?
choices: bind() is the call that sends the first datagram
Clients reach the server at a known port (12000), so the server can't let the OS pick an arbitrary port
The client's operating system doesn't allow bind()
bind() converts the server's host name to an IP address
questions.explain: Clients send to the server's known port, so the server binds its socket to port 12000. The client can accept whatever port the OS assigns.

questions.q: The UDP client calls clientSocket.sendto(message.encode(), (serverName, serverPort)), where serverName is a host name, not an IP address. Where is the name converted to an IP address?
choices: In the server, after the datagram arrives
Inside the sendto() call, which does a DNS lookup
Nowhere: UDP datagrams are routed by host name
In a bind() call the client made earlier
questions.explain: sendto() resolves the host name to an IP address for you, using DNS.

questions.q: What has to be true before a TCP client can contact a server?
choices: The server process is already running
The server has created a welcoming socket for clients to contact
The server has already created a connection socket for that client
The client has bound its socket to the server's port number
questions.explain: The server has to be running and must already have a welcoming (listening) socket. The connection socket for a client is created only after that client makes contact.

questions.q: When a new client contacts a TCP server, what does the server's TCP do?
choices: Sends all of that client's data through the welcoming socket
Closes the welcoming socket until the client disconnects
Gives the client a new well-known port number
Creates a new socket dedicated to communicating with that particular client
questions.explain: Each time a client makes contact, server TCP creates a new socket for talking to that client. This lets the server talk with several clients at once.

questions.q: What port number does the new socket created for a TCP client (the connection socket) have?
choices: A random port chosen by the server's OS
The client's port number
The same port number as the welcoming (listening) socket
The welcoming socket's port number plus one
questions.explain: The connection socket has the same port number as the welcoming socket. Connections are told apart by the client's IP address and port (demultiplexing, covered in Chapter 3).

questions.q: Many clients connect to the same port on a TCP server. What is used to tell their connections apart?
choices: Each client's source IP address and port number
The order in which the clients connected
The size of each client's first message
Each client's DNS name
questions.explain: The client's source port number and IP address distinguish the connections.

questions.q: After accept() returns, the TCP server should send its reply through the welcoming socket (serverSocket).
questions.explain: The server talks to the client through the new socket that accept() returns (connectionSocket). The welcoming socket only receives the first contact from clients.

questions.q: A TCP server like the one in the example has just returned from accept() for its first client. How many sockets does the server process have open now?
questions.explain: It has two: the welcoming socket (serverSocket) and the connection socket that accept() created for this client.

questions.q: The server calls accept() on its welcoming socket, and no client has connected yet. What happens?
choices: accept() returns None right away
The call blocks: the server waits inside accept() until a client connects
accept() raises an error
The server sends a connection request to all known clients
questions.explain: accept() is a blocking call. The server waits in it until a client connects, and then it returns the new connection socket.

questions.q: The handshake messages that set up a TCP connection are sent by the transport layer in the operating system, not by the application code.
questions.explain: The handshake happens behind the scenes in TCP. When the client's connect() returns, the connection is already established.

questions.q: How many sockets does the TCP client in the example create?
choices: Two: a welcoming socket and a connection socket
One per message it sends
One: clientSocket, which it uses both to connect and to exchange messages
None: it uses the server's socket
questions.explain: The client creates only clientSocket. The welcoming-socket/connection-socket split exists only on the server side.

questions.q: In the example TCP server, once connectionSocket.close() has been called, the server can't accept any new clients.
questions.explain: close() closes only the connection to this client. The welcoming socket stays open, so the loop goes back to accept() and waits for the next client.

questions.q: What does serverSocket.listen(1) do in the TCP server?
choices: Reads one message from the client
Binds the socket to port 1
Makes the welcoming socket start listening for incoming TCP connection requests
Accepts exactly one client and then shuts the server down
questions.explain: listen() puts the welcoming socket into listening mode so it can accept connection requests. It comes after bind() and before accept().

questions.q: Which socket method does the TCP client call to set up the connection to the server before it sends any data?
questions.explain: clientSocket.connect((serverName, serverPort)). When it returns, the connection is established.

questions.q: Which method, called on the TCP server's welcoming socket, returns a new socket for communicating with a client?
questions.explain: connectionSocket, addr = serverSocket.accept(). It waits for a client and returns the new connection socket.

questions.q: The TCP client calls clientSocket.send(sentence.encode()) without naming the server, while the UDP client's sendto() includes (serverName, serverPort). Why?
choices: TCP always sends to port 12000 by default
send() broadcasts to every host on the network
encode() stored the server's name inside the message
The TCP connection is already established, so the destination is known
questions.explain: A connected TCP socket is attached to one particular peer, so there's no need to attach the server name and port to each send.

questions.q: In the examples, how is UDP's recvfrom() different from TCP's recv()?
choices: recv() returns the data and the sender's address; recvfrom() returns only the data
recvfrom() returns the data and the sender's address; recv() returns only the data
recvfrom() works only on the server side
Only the server can call recv()
questions.explain: UDP needs the sender's address in order to reply, so recvfrom() returns (message, address). On a TCP connection socket, recv() returns just the bytes.

questions.q: In what order does the example TCP server make its socket calls?
choices: socket, listen, bind, accept, send, recv, close
socket, bind, listen, accept, recv, send, close
socket, accept, bind, listen, recv, send, close
socket, connect, bind, recv, send, close
questions.explain: Create the welcoming socket, bind it to port 12000, listen, then loop: accept a client, recv its sentence, send the uppercased sentence back, and close the connection socket.

questions.q: Which calls appear in the TCP server example but not in the UDP server example?
choices: listen()
accept()
bind()
socket()
sendto()
questions.explain: Both servers call socket() and bind(). Only the TCP server calls listen() and accept(). sendto() appears in the UDP server, not the TCP one.

questions.q: The server calls bind() on port 12000 while another process is already using that port. What happens?
choices: The two processes share the port and split the incoming data
The OS quietly assigns a different port
bind() fails with an error
The other process is terminated
questions.explain: bind() returns an error if the port is already in use. The example code doesn't check for this, although real code should.

questions.q: A student changes the UDP client's socket to socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM) and leaves the rest of the UDP client code alone. Which step from the TCP client is still missing before data can be sent?
choices: Calling clientSocket.listen(1)
Calling clientSocket.accept()
Calling clientSocket.bind(('', 12000))
Calling clientSocket.connect((serverName, serverPort))
questions.explain: A TCP client has to connect() to the server before sending. listen() and accept() are server-side calls.

questions.q: Why do the examples call .encode() before sending and .decode() after receiving?
choices: Sockets send and receive bytes, so strings are converted to bytes and back
To encrypt the message for security
To compress the message
To add the server's address to the message
questions.explain: The socket carries bytes. encode() turns the string into bytes for sending, and decode() turns the received bytes back into a string.

questions.q: In the TCP server example, which variable holds the welcoming socket?
choices: connectionSocket
serverSocket
addr
clientSocket
questions.explain: serverSocket = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM) is the welcoming socket that gets bound and listens. connectionSocket is the per-client socket that accept() returns.

questions.q: A program has to wait for replies from several different open sockets. Which approach does the material suggest?
choices: settimeout() on its own
bind() the program to several ports
select() or multithreading
listen() with a larger number
questions.explain: To wait for either a reply or a timeout, use a timer (settimeout()). To wait for replies from several sockets, use select() or multithreading.

questions.q: A program calls s.settimeout(30) and then s.recv(), and no packet arrives within 30 seconds. What happens?
choices: recv() returns an empty message and the program continues normally
recv() is interrupted and a timeout exception is raised
The socket closes itself and reopens
recv() keeps waiting until a packet arrives
questions.explain: When the timer runs out, recv() is interrupted and raises a timeout exception. The program can catch it with try/except.

questions.q: settimeout() applies only to the next operation on the socket, so it has to be called again before every recv().
questions.explain: settimeout() sets a timeout on all future operations of that particular socket. The timer starts again each time recv() is called.

questions.q: A program calls s.settimeout(10). At t = 0 s it calls s.recv(), and a message arrives at t = 4 s. At t = 6 s it calls s.recv() again, and no packet ever arrives. At what time t, in seconds, is the timeout exception raised?
questions.explain: The timer stops when the first message arrives and starts again with the second recv() at t = 6. Ten seconds with no packet after that gives t = 16.

questions.q: In a try-except block, when does the except block run?
choices: Always, after the try block finishes
Only if the named exception is raised while the try block runs
Before the try block, to set up the handler
Only if the try block finishes without errors
questions.explain: The except block runs only if the named exception occurs during the try block. Otherwise it is skipped.

questions.q: An exception is raised partway through a try block. What happens to the rest of the statements in the try block?
choices: They run first, and then the except block runs
The try block starts over from the top
They run after the except block finishes
They are skipped, and execution jumps directly into the except block
questions.explain: When an exception is raised, execution jumps straight to the matching except block. The rest of the try block doesn't run.

questions.q: In the villagers' TCP server (shepherd boy example), when does the 10-second timer start?
choices: When connectionSocket.settimeout(10) is called
When serverSocket.listen(1) is called
When connectionSocket.recv() is called
When serverSocket.accept() returns
questions.explain: settimeout(10) only sets the limit. The timer starts when recv() is called, and the timeout exception is raised if no message arrives within 10 seconds.

questions.q: In the villagers' server, what makes the while counter < 3 loop end?
choices: Three successful wolf reports
The boy closing his client socket once
Three timeouts, meaning the boy connected three times without sending a wolf location within 10 seconds
Ten connections from any client
questions.explain: counter goes up only in the except timeout branch. After three timeouts the loop ends, and the villagers stop listening.

questions.q: In the villagers' server, the boy connects and sends a wolf location within 10 seconds. What happens to counter?
choices: It goes up by 1
It is reset to 0
It goes down by 1
It stays the same: a hunter is sent and the connection is closed
questions.explain: No timeout occurs, so the try block finishes (send_hunter and the reply), the except block is skipped, and only the connection socket is closed.

questions.q: In the villagers' server, settimeout(10) is called on connectionSocket. How does this affect serverSocket.accept()?
choices: It doesn't: accept() on the welcoming socket still waits for a client with no timeout
accept() also times out after 10 seconds
accept() times out after 30 seconds
accept() is disabled until the connection socket closes
questions.explain: A timeout applies to future operations on that specific socket only. Here that is the connection socket, not the welcoming socket.

questions.q: Which of these were named as important themes of the application-layer chapter?
choices: Centralized vs. decentralized
Stateless vs. stateful
Scalability
Reliable vs. unreliable message transfer
Complexity at the network edge
Making routing decisions hop by hop in the network core
questions.explain: The themes were: client/server request/reply, centralized vs. decentralized, stateless vs. stateful, scalability, reliable vs. unreliable message transfer, and complexity at the network edge.

questions.q: What does the theme "complexity at the network edge" mean?
choices: Complexity goes into the end hosts rather than into the routers and switches deep inside the network
Routers at the edge of an ISP carry out most of the application logic
Edge networks have more complicated physical cabling than the core
Applications should avoid complex protocols at the edge
questions.explain: Over and over, the chapter's applications put their complexity in the hosts at the edge, not in the network core.

questions.q: In the sample SMTP interaction, how does the client mark the end of the message body after the DATA command?
choices: It sends the QUIT command
It sends an empty line
It sends a line containing only a period (.)
It waits for a 250 reply
questions.explain: The server's 354 reply says to "end with '.' on a line by itself". After the client sends the lone period, the server replies "250 Message accepted for delivery".

questions.q: In the sample SMTP interaction, what is the first command the client sends after the server's 220 greeting?
choices: MAIL FROM
HELO
RCPT TO
DATA
questions.explain: The sequence is HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, the message lines, ".", and finally QUIT.

questions.q: Bob's local DNS server resolves http://netcinema.com/6Y7B23V, and the video is stored on the KingCDN CDN. What does netcinema's authoritative DNS server return?
choices: The IP address of netcinema.com's web server
A CNAME pointing to a KingCDN.com name for the video
The video file itself
The address of Bob's local DNS server
questions.explain: Netcinema's authoritative DNS returns a CNAME for the KingCDN.com name. KingCDN's authoritative DNS then resolves that name to a KingCDN server, and Bob streams the video from that server over HTTP.

questions.q: In the Netflix case study, what does Bob's client receive for the chosen video before it contacts a CDN server and starts streaming with DASH?
choices: The full video file from the Amazon cloud
A CNAME record from Bob's local DNS
Account details from the registration servers
A manifest file for that specific video
questions.explain: Bob browses videos (Amazon cloud), receives the manifest file for the video he picks, and then a DASH server (a CDN server) is chosen and contacted, and streaming begins.
